Revelation 17:1 The state of the Church militant being declared, now followeth the state of the Church overcoming and getting victory, as I showed before in the beginning of chapter 10. The state is set forth in 4 chapters. As in the place beforegoing I noted, that in that history the order of time was not always exactly observed, so the same is to be understood in this history, that it is distinguished according to the persons of which it treateth, and that in the several stories of the persons is severly observed in the time thereof. For first is delivered the story of Babylon destroyed, in this and the next chap. (for this Babylon out of all doubt shall perish before the 2 beasts and the Dragon). Secondly is delivered the destruction of both the two beasts, chap. 19. And lastly of the Dragon, chap. 20, in the story of the spiritual Babylon are distinctly set forth the state thereof in this chap. and the overthrow done from God, chap. 18. In this verse and that which followeth is a transition or passage unto the first argument, consisting of a particular calling of the Prophet (as often heretofore) and a general proposition.
Revelation 17:1 That is the damnable harlot, by a figure of speech called hypallage. For S. John as yet had not seen her. Although another interpretation may be borne, yet I like this better.
Revelation 17:1 The sentence that is pronounced against this harlot.
Revelation 17:3 Henceforth is propounded the type of Babylon, and the state thereof in 4 verses. After a declaration of the type, in the rest of this chap., in the type are described two things, the beast (of whom chap. 13), in verse 3, and the woman that sitteth upon the beast, verses 4, 5, 6. The beast in process of time hath gotten somewhat more than was expressed in the former vision. First in that it is not read before that he was appareled in scarlet, a robe imperial and of triumph. Secondly, in that this is full of names of blasphemy: the other carried the name of blasphemy only in his head. So God did teach that this beast is much increased in impiety and injustice and doth in this last age, triumph in both these more insolently and proudly than ever before.
Revelation 17:3 A scarlet color, that is, with a red and purple garment: and surely it was not without cause that the Romish clergy were so much delighted with this color.
Revelation 17:4 That harlot, the spiritual Babylon, which is Rome. She is described by her attire, profession and deeds.
Revelation 17:4 In attire most glorious, triumphant, most rich, and most gorgeous.
Revelation 17:4 In profession, the nourisher of all, in this verse, and teaching her mysteries unto all, verse 5, setting forth all things most magnificently: but indeed most pernicious besotting miserable men with her cup, and bringing upon them a deadly giddiness.
Revelation 17:5 Deceiving with the title of religion, and public inscription of mystery: which the beast in times past did not bear.
Revelation 17:5 An exposition: in which S. John declareth what manner of woman this is.
Revelation 17:6 In manner of deeds: She is red with blood, and sheddeth it most licentiously, and therefore is colored with the blood of the Saints, as on the contrary part. Christ is set forth imbrued with the blood of his enemies; Isa. 3:1.
Revelation 17:6 A passage unto the second part of this chapter, by occasion given of S. John, as the words of the Angel do show, in the next verse.
Revelation 17:7 The second part or place, as I said, verse 1. The narration of the vision, promised in this verse, and delivered in the verse following. Now there is delivered first a narration of the beast and his story, unto verse 14. After, of the harlot, unto the end of the chap.
Revelation 17:8 The story of the beast hath a triple description of him. The first is a distinction of this beast from all that ever hath been at any time: which distinction is contained in this verse: The second is a delineation or painting out of the beast by things present, by which he might even at that time be known of the godly, and this delineation is according to his heads, verses 2, 10, 11. The third is an historical foretelling of things to come, and to be done by him: and these are ascribed unto his horns, verses 12, 13, 14. This beast is that Empire of Rome, of which I spake, chap. 13:11, according to the mutations and changes whereof which then had already happened, the holy Ghost hath distinguished and set out the same. The Apostle distinguisheth this beast from all others in these words. The beast which thou sawest, was and is not. For so I expound the words of the Apostle for evidence’s sake as I will further declare in the notes following.
Revelation 17:8 The meaning is, that beast which thou sawest before (Rev. 13:1) and which yet thou hast now seen, was, (I say was) even from Julius Caesar in respect of beginning, rising up, station, glory, dominion, manner and stock, from the house of Julius: and yet is not now the same, if thou look unto the house and stock for the dominion of this family was translated unto another, after the death of Nero from the other unto a third, from a third unto a fourth, and so forth was varied and altered by innumerable changes. Finally, the Empire is one, as it were one beast: but exceedingly varied by kindreds, families, and persons. It was therefore (saith S. John) in the kindred or house of Julius: and now it is not in that kindred, but translated unto another.
Revelation 17:8 As if he should say, Also the same that is, shall shortly not be: but shall ascend out of the depth, or out of the sea (as was said, Rev. 13:1) that is, shall be a new stock from amongst the nations without difference, and shall in the same state go unto destruction or ruin, and perish: and so shall successively new Princes or Emperors come and go, arise and fall, the body of the beast remaining still, but tossed with so many and often alterations, as no man can but marvel that this beast was able to stand and hold out, in so many mutations. Verily no Empire that ever was tossed with so many changes, and as it were with so many tempests of the sea, ever continued so long.
Revelation 17:8 That is as many as have not learned the providence of God, according to the faith of the Saints, shall marvel at these grievous and often changes when they shall consider, the selfsame beast, which is the Roman Empire, to have been, not to be, and to be and still molested with perpetual mutation, and yet in the same to stand and continue. This in mine opinion is the most simple exposition of this place, and confirmed by the event of the things themselves. Although by the last change also, by which the Empire, that before was civil became Ecclesiastical, is not obscurely signified by these words: of which two, the first exercised cruelty upon the bodies of the saints: the other also upon their souls: the first by human order and policy, the other under the color of the law of God, and of Religion, raged and imbrued itself with the blood of the godly.
Revelation 17:9 An exhortation preparing unto audience, by the same argument, with that of Christ: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Wherefore, for mine own part, I had rather read in this place, Let there be here a mind, etc. So the Angel passeth fully unto the second place of this description.
Revelation 17:9 Very children know what that seven hilled city is, which is so much spoken of, and whereof Virgil thus reporteth, And compasseth seven towers in one wall: that city it is, which when John wrote these things had rule over the kings of the earth: It was and is not, and yet it remaineth this day, but it is declining to destruction.
Revelation 17:9 This is the painting out of the beast by things present (as I said before) whereby S. John endeavored to describe the same, that he might both be known of the godly in that age, and be further observed and marked of posterity afterwards. This delineation hath one type, that is, his heads, but a double description or application of the type: one permanent from the nature of itself, the other changeable, by the working of men. The description permanent, is by the seven hills, in this verse, the other that fleeteth, is from the seven kings, verses 10, 11. And here it is worthy to be observed, that one type hath sometimes two or more applications, as seemeth good unto the holy Ghost to express either one thing by divers types, or divers things by one type. So I noted before, of the seven spirits, Rev. 1:4. Now this woman that sitteth upon seven hills, is the city of Rome, called in times past of the Greeks, … i. of seven tops or crests, and of Varro, septiceps, i. of her seven heads (as here) of seven heads, and of others, septicollis, i. standing upon seven hills.
Revelation 17:9 The beginning of these Kings or Emperors is almost the same with the beginning of the Church of Christ, which I showed before, Rev. 11:1. Namely from the year 35, after the passion of Christ, what time the Temple and Church of the Jews was overthrown. In which year it came to pass by the providence of God that that saying The beast was and is not, was fulfilled before that the destruction of the Jews immediately following came to pass. That was the year from the building of the city of Rome, 109, from which year S. John both numbered the Emperors which hitherto hath been, when he wrote these things, and foretelleth two others next to come: and that with this purpose, that when this particular prediction of foretelling of things to come, should take effect the truth of all other predictions in the Church might be the more confirmed. Which sign God of old mentioned this in the Law, Deut. 18, and Jeremiah confirmeth, Jer. 28:8.
Revelation 17:10 Whose names are these: the first, Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was the seventh Emperor of the people of Rome, the second Marcus Salvius Otho, the third Aulus Vitellius, the fourth, Titus Flavius Vespasianus, the fifth, Titus Vespasianus his son of his own name.

text:
A seventeen-year-old boy stepped on his own daddy's hand in the dark. He had been trying to start his father's truck, and his father was lying underneath it by the gate, a few hours before the two of them were supposed to leave Mississippi for good. When the sheriff came out that night he went through the dead man's wallet, right there in front of the boy, and he took something out of it.

It was going on eleven o'clock on the night of Friday, January 31, 1964, and Hank Allen was seventeen years old and driving home from a party in Gloster.

His cousin John Horton was in the passenger seat, sixteen. The car was a 1954 DeSoto and the road was Highway 24, running east toward Liberty, Mississippi.

Hank made the left into his family's driveway and drove up toward the gap.

That was what they called the gate his father had built into the barbed wire, the one that kept the chickens and the mules from wandering off the place. His father's bobtailed Ford logging truck was sitting just outside it, engine off, headlights burning.

Hank could not think why his daddy would leave the truck across the driveway like that.

He got out and called for him. Nothing came back, so he walked around the truck and climbed up into the cab and turned the key, thinking maybe the battery had gone flat and his father had walked up to the house for help.

The battery had gone flat.

He climbed back down, and coming off the running board his foot came down on something in the dark that was not ground.

It was his father's right hand.

Hank backed the DeSoto up and put the headlights under the truck. Louis Allen was lying face down beside his own front gate, forty-four years old, and he had been dead for a little while.

The boy went to reach for him. John caught his arm and would not let go, because John understood something Hank was not able to think about yet, which was that in Amite County a Black boy did not touch a body before the white law had seen it.

So they got back in the car and drove two miles east to the sheriff's house.

They got there near midnight. As Hank came up on Sheriff Daniel Jones's back door he heard a sound he knew, the sound of a shotgun being pumped somewhere inside.

He knocked anyway and told the sheriff that somebody had shot his father.

"Is he dead?" Jones asked him.

Hank said he hoped not. Walking back to his car he heard the shotgun pump a second time.

Here is who was lying under that truck.

Louis Allen was born in Amite County in April of 1919 and spent most of his childhood in the house of a prosperous white family named Aarons, because the patriarch had asked his mother for one of her boys to help around the place and she gave up the darker one. In 1943 he enlisted at Camp Shelby and went to New Guinea, where he drove ammunition trucks and learned to box.

He was five foot eight and two hundred twenty pounds and built like a door. The Army rated his character excellent, discharged him honorably in July of 1944, and handed him three hundred dollars in mustering out pay.

He came home with it and built a logging business.

He bought land, put cattle on it and vegetables in it, married a woman named Elizabeth and raised four children. He became a man white men in Liberty did business with, which in that county was a tightrope people walked their whole lives.

He walked it for sixteen years. Then, on the twenty-fifth of September, 1961, he pulled his truck into a line at a cotton gin and it came to an end.

Ahead of him in that line was a dairy farmer named Herbert Lee, who had nine children and who was one of the first Black men in Amite County to try to put his name on a voter roll. Coming toward Lee across the lot was a white man named E. H. Hurst, a member of the Mississippi House of Representatives, with a .38 in his hand.

Hurst and Lee had played together as boys, a long time ago, and it did not appear to be on either man's mind.

Lee would not talk while the gun was out. Hurst let it drop, and Lee stepped down out of his truck with his hands empty and an unlit cigarette in his mouth, and Hurst brought the gun back up and fired once.

Louis Allen and about a dozen other men stood there and watched it happen.

They did not have to wait long for the reckoning. A coroner's jury was seated that same day, in a courtroom filled with white men who had brought their guns in with them.

Before it convened, the law got to the witnesses. Louis Allen was told what he was going to say, which was that Herbert Lee had come at a state legislator with a tire iron.

He said at first that he would not swear to something he had not seen.

Then he was told that if he did not, they would kill his entire family. He had a wife and four children about three miles up the road, and so Louis Allen stood up in that room and said he had seen a tire iron in a dead man's hand.

Five men said it. The jury took no time at all and found that Representative Hurst had defended himself, and Hurst walked out of the courthouse and drove home and was never charged with anything, ever.

That should have been the end of it. Louis Allen had done what the county required and he was free to go back to hauling timber.

It was not the end of it, and the reason why is the whole story.

His wife explained it years later, in a deposition she gave to the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party in the summer of 1964. If he had told a story on a living man, Elizabeth Allen said, he could go and ask that man to forgive him.

He could not ask a dead one. So, she said, his conscience was clipping him.

It clipped him for months. Then he found Bob Moses of SNCC and told him that if somebody could keep his family safe, he would go before a federal grand jury and let the hide go with the hair.

Those were his words. SNCC carried the message to the Justice Department, and the Justice Department sent back that there was no protection available.

And then, somehow, Liberty found out he had offered.

What happened to Louis Allen after that took two years and never once required a white man in that county to break a law any other white man would enforce. His timber customers quit him one by one, until he was driving into Louisiana to buy gas and hunting work in counties far enough off that nobody had heard about him.

In June of 1962 a deputy named Daniel Jones came to the house to arrest him for interfering with an officer. Hank was there and watched his father put his wrists out to be cuffed.

Louis asked if he could have his hat.

Jones said no. Louis asked, then, whether his boy could carry the hat out to him.

What Jones did next was hit him in the face with a flashlight hard enough to break his jaw.

Two months after that, with his jaw wired, Louis Allen walked into the courthouse in Liberty and tried to register to vote. There were gunshots outside and the power went out inside, and he did not get registered, and no Black person in Amite County had been permitted to since 1890.

In November of 1963 Jones arrested him again, for carrying a weapon and for writing a check that was overdrawn by two or three dollars.

His older son Tommie did not believe his father would come out of that jail alive. He told Hank they had better make sure the old man was actually locked up and stayed that way, and then the two boys took two old guns down to the jailhouse next to the courthouse in Liberty.

They stayed there all night. One brother stood by the outhouse across from the front door watching for anybody who came, and the other slept in the car, and then they traded.

They did that for about twenty nights, until the NAACP raised eight hundred dollars and bonded him out.

After that he stopped arguing about leaving. His brother Morris was in Milwaukee and would help him find work, and Louis told his family he was tired of being picked on, which is a small phrase for what had been done to him.

His parents were old and sick and living in a house on his land, and he would not go while they needed him. His mother died on Wednesday, January 22, 1964.

He set his departure for that Saturday.

On the Friday he drove over to see a former boss of his named Lloyd King and asked him for a letter he could show a man in Wisconsin. King wrote it out by hand and Louis folded it into his pocket.

It said that Lewis Allen was a good truck driver and could run a cat, that he had worked several years for the writer, and that the writer had been pleased with his work. King spelled his name wrong.

That was the last piece of paper Louis Allen ever carried, and his name was misspelled on it.

That same evening, before he drove off, his son held the gap open for him and followed him through and closed it behind them both.

"Whatever you do, son, you look out for your mom and your little sister," Louis told him.

"Daddy's gonna go up there, go to work. In about three weeks, I'll be sending for y'all."

Then Hank went to his party in Gloster, and his father went to get his letter, and a few hours later the boy stepped on his hand in the dark.

Sheriff Daniel Jones came out to the property with a doctor. Standing over the body, in front of the dead man's teenage son, he said he would see if he could find what caused the problem.

Then he went through Louis Allen's pockets.

He took out the wallet and went through the cash, and then he went through the cards, and he came to a small one that said Louis Allen was a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. He stopped there and told Hank he would need to keep the wallet overnight.

He brought it back the next day. The NAACP card was not in it.

That is the part to hold on to, because everything after it turns on that card.

The coroner's jury Jones assembled the next morning found that Louis Allen had been killed by an assailant or assailants unknown. Jones told reporters he had no idea why anyone would want the man dead, and floated to the FBI that it might have been trouble between Louis and his wife.

The Justice Department did send agents. For ten days they interviewed Elizabeth Allen, Lloyd King, Daniel Jones and others around Liberty.

Elizabeth told them her husband had not been involved in voter registration work.

Understand what she was doing. Her husband was in the ground, the sheriff who had broken his jaw was running the investigation, and she had children left in that house who could still be killed.

Hank had driven his father to NAACP meetings himself, out in the woods outside Liberty where Black men taught each other to read and write. He used to flick his headlights on and off before he pulled up, in case anybody was following.

The FBI wrote its report and closed the file. It concluded that the victim was not a registered voter, had never been active in voter registration work, and that there had been no voter registration activity in Amite County in the past two or three years.

All three statements were true, and the reason all three were true is the reason he was dead.

On the morning of Saturday, February 1, the Council of Federated Organizations was in the middle of a staff meeting in Hattiesburg. They had spent months arguing over a proposal to bring a large number of white northern college students into Mississippi that summer, and they were getting nowhere with it.

The meeting was interrupted by a phone call from Amite County.

Bob Moses had stayed mostly quiet through that argument. After the call he stopped being quiet, and afterward he said only that it had become clear they had to do something big enough to open the situation up.

They already knew what would open it, and that is the part that never makes the anniversary posts.

Herbert Lee had been killed by a sitting state legislator in front of a dozen witnesses and the country had not turned its head. Louis Allen had been killed at his own gate and the country had not turned its head.

So they built a summer out of that fact. Bring down white students from good families in New York and California, and when Mississippi did to those students what it had been doing to people like Louis Allen for ninety years, the cameras would come, and the federal government would follow the cameras.

Grown people sat in a room and decided to use their own country's racism as a lever, because nothing else had ever moved it.

Volunteers began arriving at a small women's college in Oxford, Ohio on June 14, somewhere between seven hundred and a thousand of them. On the lawns they were taught how to fall and cover their heads, while SNCC and CORE staff rolled up sleeves and showed them the scars.

Six days after the first group crossed into Mississippi, it worked.

James Chaney, a Black CORE worker from Meridian, drove out with Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner to look at a burned church in Neshoba County. A deputy arrested the three of them, held them, and turned them loose after dark.

Within days the President was involved, sailors were walking the swamps, and it was on every front page in America.

And while they dragged the rivers looking for two white men and one Black man, they kept bringing up people nobody had been looking for.

On July 12, in a channel of the Mississippi down near Natchez, the search brought up a body that was none of the three. The next day it brought up another.

They were Henry Hezekiah Dee and Charles Eddie Moore, both about nineteen, who had been hitchhiking outside Meadville on the second of May when Klansmen picked them up on the wrong assumption that they were organizers. Neither one had ever been in the movement, and they had been gone ten weeks, and no search had ever been sent out for them.

There was a fourteen-year-old boy, Herbert Oarsby, found in a CORE shirt. There were five more men who were never identified and never will be.

Once it was clear these were not the bodies the country was watching for, the reporters packed up.

Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner were found on August 4 under an earthen dam, forty-four days gone. Michael Schwerner's widow Rita was twenty-two years old, and she stood in front of the press and would not let them make it into something clean.

The killing of a Black man in Mississippi was not news, she told them. The alarm had been sounded only because her husband and Andrew Goodman were white.

She was not being bitter, she was reading the plan back to them out loud, and she had more right to say it than anybody standing there.

Measured against the thing it said it was doing, the summer failed. Around seventeen thousand Black Mississippians went to a courthouse that summer and filled out the form, and about sixteen hundred of them ended up on the rolls.

The rest of the ledger runs like this. One thousand and sixty-two arrests, eighty workers beaten, thirty-seven churches bombed or burned, thirty homes and businesses the same, four civil rights workers killed, and at least three local Black Mississippians killed for their part in it.

One column came out ahead. Around forty Freedom Schools opened, and more than three thousand children and grown folks came through them to study reading, civics, and their own history for the first time in their lives.

And on August 22 a sharecropper's daughter from Ruleville sat down in front of the Democratic Party's credentials committee in Atlantic City, gave her name, and then gave her home address out loud on national television.

Mississippi had written its laws specifically to make that information deadly. Fannie Lou Hamer said it into a microphone on purpose.

The President of the United States called an emergency press conference to pull the networks off her. They ran her that night anyway, in full, and the mail came in by the sack.

Louis Allen had been in the ground about seven months by then.

They buried him on a Monday morning at Star Hill Baptist Church, and Hank says the building could not hold half the people who came. That same evening Elizabeth put her son and her little girl Mary in a car and took them across the line into Louisiana, to relatives, because she did not believe the house was survivable anymore.

Hank was seventeen and there was no money. He hooked scrap iron out of the Mississippi River for eight dollars a day for six months, until his mother made him go back and finish his senior year on the grounds that his father would have wanted the diploma.

Almost exactly a year after the gate, he came home one evening and found her frightened. She had dreamed that men in Liberty were coming to kill him, and she told him he had to go north.

He left that same night, caught a train out of New Orleans, and rode it to Milwaukee.

Sit with that. The trip Louis Allen was packed for, the one he was going to send for his family in three weeks to join, was finally made by his son, one year later, running.

Nobody has ever been arrested for it. The FBI reopened the case in 2006 with Daniel Jones as its subject, and the Justice Department finally closed the file in May of 2015, under a heading that reads Daniel Jones, Deceased.

In 1988, Louis Allen's grandson Kevin heard that Jones was still alive and working at a hardware store in Liberty. He drove there, walked in past the barrel of ax handles by the door, and stood in front of the old sheriff.

"You thought you killed Louis Allen," Kevin told him, "but you multiplied him. There was one, now there are several."

Then he walked out and drove off, and he says Jones grabbed at his chest and did not say one word.

There is a boy in that family now, a great-grandson, who boxes. Before every fight he ties on a white bandana with two gloves printed on it and four words between them, which are RIP LOUIS ALLEN.

That is a family that has been printing his name on whatever it can find for sixty-two years, because a sheriff took the only card that had it on him and the United States government wrote down that he was nobody in particular.

So print it somewhere. Louis Allen, Herbert Lee, Henry Dee, Charles Moore, Herbert Oarsby, and the five men out of the river who were never given a name at all.

His stone is out on Old Compromise Road, and the silver paint on the letters has gone dull.

Louis Allen's story was almost buried inside a file number, a missing card, and a forgotten grave. I share stories like his because sometimes the first step toward justice is simply making sure people know the name.

text:
81. Thirukkadithalam (Thrikodithanam Mahavishnu Temple)

Location: Kottayam district, Kerala
Deities: Sri Amruthanarayana Perumal & Goddess Karpagavalli Thayar
Significance: According to legend, this ancient temple is believed to have been built by Sahadeva, the youngest of the Pandava brothers. The deity here is praised for granting structural peace and fulfilling sincere prayers. 

82. Thiruchengundrur (Thrichittatt Maha Vishnu Temple)

Location: Chengannur, Alappuzha district, Kerala
Deities: Sri Devathideva Perumal (Imayavarappan) & Goddess Rakthapankajavalli Thayar
Significance: This temple is traditionally associated with Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava brother, who built it to seek forgiveness for speaking a white lie during the Mahabharata war. 

83. Thiruppuliyur (Thripuliyoor Mahavishnu Temple)

Location: Puliyoor, Alappuzha district, Kerala
Deities: Sri Mayashaktiyuthaswamy Perumal (Thripuliyoorappan) & Goddess Hemalatha Thayar
Significance: Believed to have been constructed by Bheema, the second Pandava brother. The temple design incorporates a unique platform honoring Bheema's legendary mace.

84. Thiruvaranvilai (Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple)

Location: Aranmula, Pathanamthitta district, Kerala
Deities: Sri Vamana Perumal (Parthasarathy) & Goddess Padmasani Thayar
Significance: Constructed by Arjuna, this temple sits beautifully on the banks of the Pamba River. It is world-famous for its traditional annual Aranmula Uthrattathi Boat Race and the sacred golden attire (Thanga Anki) delivered here. 

85. Thiruvanvandoor (Thiruvanvandoor Mahavishnu Temple)

Location: Alappuzha district, Kerala
Deities: Sri Kamalanatha Perumal (Paambanaappan) & Goddess Kamalavalli Thayar
Significance: This shrine is associated with Nakula, the fourth Pandava brother. Legend has it that Sage Narada composed the Naradiya Purana at this precise, tranquil location. 

86. Thiruvananthapuram (Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple)

Location: Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala
Deities: Sri Ananthapadmanabha Perumal & Goddess Harilakshmi Thayar
Significance: The richest Hindu temple in the world, featuring Lord Vishnu in a majestic reclining (Ananthasayana) posture over the giant serpent Adisesha. The massive deity can be viewed through three distinct structural doors representing different stages of cosmic life. 

87. Thiruvattaru (Sri Adikesava Perumal Temple)

Location: Thiruvattar, Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu
Deities: Sri Adhikesava Perumal & Goddess Maragadhavalli Thayar
Significance: The primary deity is exceptionally grand, measuring 22 feet long in a reclining position. Structurally and mythologically, it predates and strongly shares common traditions with the Thiruvananthapuram Padmanabhaswamy temple. 

88. Thiruvanparisaram (Sri Thiruvazhmarbhan Temple)

Location: Thiruppathisaram, Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu
Deities: Sri Thiruvazhmarbhan Perumal & Goddess Kamalavalli Thayar
Significance: The name translates to "the place where the Lord holds Lakshmi in His chest." It holds deep spiritual history as the historical birthplace of Udayanangai, the mother of the famous Vaishnavite saint Nammalvar. 

89. Thirukkurungudi (Azhagiya Nambi Temple)

Location: Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu
Deities: Sri Vamanakshetrapoornaya Perumal (Azhagiya Nambi) & Goddess Vamanaksetravalli Thayar
Significance: Known as a Dakshina Badrikashramam, Lord Vishnu is said to have taught structural spiritual concepts to Sage Markandeya here. It is highly celebrated for the traditional Kaisika Ekadasi dance-drama festival. 

90. Thirucheeravaramangai (Vanamamalai / Nanguneri Totadri Perumal Temple)

Location: Nanguneri, Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu
Deities: Sri Thothadhrinatha Perumal & Goddess Chireevaramangaivalli Thayar
Significance: One of the eight Swayamvyaktha Kshetras (self-manifested shrines) of Lord Vishnu. The temple features a holy oil well (Ennai Kinaru); the oil offered to the deity accumulates here and is known to possess natural therapeutic properties.

There are sacred places where the pursuit of knowledge becomes a form of worship. Sringeri in Karnataka is one such kshetra.

The Sri Sharadamba Temple is closely associated with Adi Shankaracharya, who established the Sringeri Sharada Peetham as a centre of Advaita Vedanta.

Goddess Sharadamba, worshipped here as the embodiment of knowledge and wisdom, holds a special place in the spiritual heritage of Bharat.

During Navaratri, devotees offer their prayers to Sharadamba, seeking not merely knowledge, but the wisdom to understand ourselves, discern the Truth and walk the path of Dharma.

May Devi illuminate our minds, guide our thoughts and lead us towards true wisdom.

Denver Nuggets forward Spencer Jones is progressing toward a return from a hamstring injury and could be available for Thursday's season opener against the Oklahoma City Thunder.

• Jones missed Denver's entire preseason after suffering a left hamstring strain during team practices. He participated in Sunday's practice and said his recovery is progressing toward opening night.

• The 25-year-old averaged 5.5 points per game on 50.4% shooting last season, making 37 starts. He increased his scoring average to 6.5 points in the playoffs and shot 69.2% from three-point range.

• Denver matched Oklahoma City's reported two-year, $12 million offer sheet in July to retain Jones. His potential return would provide additional wing depth with Julian Strawther sidelined by a left knee sprain.

Jones said his opening-night availability is not yet guaranteed, but he expects to be ready if his recovery continues as planned. Denver opens its season Thursday against the defending NBA champion Thunder.

text:
This argument makes absolutely no sense. Joe Kelly is confusing a team salary cap with an individual player salary cap. They’re two completely different things.

He’s basically saying that if every team could only pay Ohtani the same amount, he’d automatically choose the Dodgers because they win, have great weather, etc. and apparently every other superstar would do the same and just line up to play for LA or New York. Really?

that’s not how a salary cap works. The whole point of a team cap, along with a salary floor, is to prevent wealthy teams from simply outspending everyone else and stockpiling the best players while forcing smaller market teams to spend enough to remain competitive.

let’s play this out. Say the cap is $250 million per team. The Dodgers are already at $245 million and Tarik Skubal is a free agent. LA can offer him $5 million, while Pittsburgh or Milwaukee has the room to offer him $40 million.

according to Kelly’s logic, Skubal is just going to turn down an additional $35 million PER YEAR to play for the Dodgers because he likes winning and the weather? Come on, that’s ridiculous.

a salary cap doesn’t mean every player makes the same amount. It means teams have to make choices about how they allocate their money. That’s what creates competitive balance and prevents a handful of teams from collecting all the top talent.

where exactly did Joe Kelly get his economics education?

text:
Can that shift alone put a country behind? Yes, absolutely. History shows that scientific supremacy isn't static; it follows prestige, institutional trust, and talent accumulation. If entering pure science in the U.S. means enduring 7 years of low-paid graduate or postdoc work, brutal grant bureaucracy, and low social visibility while Wall Street, management consulting, and algorithmic ad-tech offer immediate wealth and status the domestic talent pipeline shifts away from physical breakthroughs. China has already surpassed the West in total publication volume, patent filings, and output in premier scientific indices, such as the Nature Index. When a rival nation pairs cultural veneration with massive capital, it creates an environment where breakthrough discovery accelerates exponentially.

​A society ultimately reflects what it celebrates. When a nation stops treating discovery and technical mastery as high civic virtues, the resulting decline in innovation doesn't happen overnight—it erodes the scientific foundation until falling behind becomes an irreversible reality.
​"Science is more than searching for the unknown; it can be lost in discovery, hidden and forged in quantum fields of corruption. For if a villain conquered time, then our present is the burst and we are living in the cursed. Through understanding, unity is built; through truth and only unified, shared truths do we build progress. Supremacy isn’t won in isolation or divisions; it’s won when talent meets purpose!
​When we trade division for collaboration, our missing scientists become our greatest contributors.

​Abolish the fear, stand for truth, abolish hate, coordinate! 👊"
​— Julian Sapp

text:
How you respond to Delta, Amazon, and others blocking agents is almost a litmus test for which side of the map you’re on

If you’re a technologist your response is probably “agents are inevitable and businesses blocking them will lose”. You most likely underestimate the friction involved and how long it will take to untangle (plus nothing is inevitable)

If you’re a business outside of tech, this is probably a headache for you (blocking is the easiest decision right now, and you don’t get a lot from this trend). But you most likely underestimate how much traffic agents will drive five years from now.

But there’s a lot of nuance missing from these viral tweets:

- There’s still very little volume in agentic commerce (low single-digit billions of dollars). So most businesses outside of pure tech cannot model the upside right now

- There’s not enough evidence that users actually want agents to handle the “last mile” (checkout). The trust issue alone might take years until users are educated enough to make businesses care.

- Much of big commerce depends on ads/ upsells/ or both, and businesses have strong incentives to maintain the first-party customer relationship. There is a reason why most of the MCP Apps do not cover the last mile

These three points mean this won’t be easy to untangle. We can expect a mixed experience with agentic commerce for the next few years imo (meaning there will still be much better prices, terms and inventory outside of agents in many type of commerce fields)

In the meantime, if you’re building an agent with commerce capabilities, two things to keep in mind:

1) Respect the business. Let businesses offer upsells and give users the option to co-browse the last mile rather than forcing everything into a headless flow.

2) Respect the terms. Make sure users are presented with relevant terms and conditions before committing to a purchase.

The dynamic of power will show agent developers that much of this is in the realm of business/ collaboration and not pure tech. And the biggest reward will be towards companies that can find the middle ground with the other side and not brute force

US TECH FUTURES ARE REBOUNDING. BUT THE CONCERNS BEHIND THE AI SELLOFF HAVEN'T DISAPPEARED.
WHAT I'M WATCHING — MONDAY, OCTOBER 19
Nasdaq futures are recovering after last week's sharp technology sell-off, while Asian markets are still struggling.
What interests me is that the underlying concerns haven't really changed.
THE MARKET PICTURE
▪ Nasdaq futures: +1.0%
▪ S&P 500 futures: +0.7%
▪ Japan's Nikkei: −1.2%
▪ South Korea's KOSPI: −0.4%
▪ Brent crude: $107.95, down 1.7%
▪ US 10-year Treasury yield: 5.05%
Early-session market snapshot.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11.4% last week as investors questioned whether the enormous investment going into AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
CHINA'S ECONOMY IS HOLDING UP BETTER THAN EXPECTED
China's economy grew 4.5% in Q3, slightly ahead of the 4.4% forecast.
▪ Industrial production: +5.5% YoY in September
▪ Retail sales: +1.1% YoY in September
▪ Property development investment: −20.6% over January–September
Encouraging numbers, but the recovery remains uneven.
Manufacturing and exports are helping support growth, while property investment and domestic consumption remain weak.
HERE'S WHAT I'M WATCHING
Oil prices are falling, Treasury yields are easing, and that's giving US stock futures some breathing room.
But lower Treasury yields don't suddenly make every AI investment profitable.
Companies are spending billions building data centres, buying GPUs and securing power.
AI infrastructure demand remains substantial, particularly among major technology companies.
What's less certain is how much of that demand eventually translates into sustainable earnings and free cash flow.
That's why I'm watching $CRWV, $IREN and $NBIS closely.
All three have significant AI infrastructure exposure, but their financing requirements, execution risks and potential shareholder returns are different.
THIS WEEK'S EARNINGS MATTER
I'll be watching $META and $LRCX particularly closely for what they say about AI spending, infrastructure demand and margins.
Results from $TSLA and $TXN will also offer a broader view of business conditions.
For me, the key isn't simply whether companies beat expectations.
It's what management says about demand, spending and the returns they're getting on that investment.
MY TAKEAWAY
I welcome the rebound in technology futures, but I'm not convinced investors have finished questioning the economics of AI infrastructure.
A few strong trading sessions won't settle that debate.
The next phase of the AI trade isn't just about who can spend the most. It's about who can turn that spending into sustainable earnings, free cash flow and shareholder returns.
— EMMANUELINVEST

text:
The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born — The Gleam and the Governor  
19 Oct 2026, 4:15 a.m.

Note the spelling. Armah wrote “Beautyful” on purpose. He wanted the eye to trip so the mind would notice what the country had learned to live inside.

His 1968 novel is not Ghanaian. It is a Nigerian novel that happened to be written in Ghana. A man with no name works the railway. He will not take the envelope. Everyone around him treats the refusal as a kind of sickness. His wife Oyo does not demand luxury. She asks why he will not act like a normal man. Other husbands bring home the gleam. He brings home only the news that he has said no again. 

On the latrine walls,
the graffiti is already philosophy: Money Sweet Pass All. 

The walls themselves will not flush. The rot does not apologise. It simply accumulates.

Minister Koomson is not a villain. He is the finished product. Flash car, house that salary cannot explain, loved because he redistributes a little of what he has taken. When the system that made him begins to hunt him, it is the nameless clerk who helps him crawl out through the latrine hole. 

Armah’s joke is precise: even the man who has refused the filth must wade through it to perform an ordinary mercy. Integrity does not redesign the sewage system. It only declines to add another blockage.

Achebe showed what happens when the centre cannot hold. 

Emecheta showed what happens when a society extracts from women more than it returns and still calls the result joy. 

Armah completes the line: independence transferred the instruments of accumulation. It did not retire them. Nigeria simply scaled the same grammar—from cocoa to crude, from gleam to oil block, from modest bribe to budget padding that now speaks the language of national interest. Every generation announces that the beautiful ones have arrived. Then the photographs surface and we discover we have hired a more fluent Koomson.

That is why the governors matter, and why they do not matter enough. In Abia, Alex Otti met a state that had turned salary arrears and ghost workers into a permanent weather. Forensic audit, no new borrowing, roughly three-quarters of the inherited debt cut, roads reappearing in places that had forgotten what a road was for. That is not Koomson. That is the man still refusing the gleam. In Oyo, Seyi Makinde has tried something rarer: to build things a successor will find expensive to reverse—Amotekun when the centre cannot secure its own citizens, institutions with actual mandates, education and liveability numbers that survive one tenure. These are real partial births. You cannot call them cosmetic.

They are also limited. 
A governor can clear arrears in Umuahia and still cannot rewrite the federal allocation formula that keeps the centre hungry. He can functionalise health centres and still cannot touch the opacity that turns oil into private wealth before it becomes public revenue. He can construct a road that lasts and still watch the national incentives produce ten new Koomsons next door. 

Peter Obi’s 2023 campaign felt, for many, like the moment the title’s promise might finally be kept at scale. 

The years since have illustrated the quieter warning: a change of driver does not repair the bus when the engine has been redesigned for leakage.

The clerk helps Koomson through the latrine because good faith alone does not dismantle the architecture. It only refuses to add to it. That is why the last image is the one that matters. 

A bus is still moving. On its side, still misspelled, still stubborn: THE BEAUTYFUL ONES ARE NOT YET BORN. 

Beside the words, someone has painted a small flower. The flower is absurd. It is also the only evidence the book offers that purity remains possible.

Abia’s debt reduction is one such flower. 

Oyo’s attempt to make integrity institutional rather than personal is another. So is the civil servant who still says no when the envelope arrives, and the voter who waits in the rain...

[CONTINUED BELOW]👇🏻

text:
4:22AM

The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born — The Gleam and The Governor

Note the spelling.
Armah wrote "Beautyful" deliberately. He wanted you to notice the error and the hope inside it.

Ayi Kwei Armah's 1968 novel is not a Ghanaian novel. It is a Nigerian novel written in Ghana.

Set in the last months of Kwame Nkrumah through the 1966 coup, it follows a man with no name. Just "the man." 

A railway clerk who refuses to take bribe.

Everyone around him thinks he is a fool.

His wife Oyo asks him: why will you not be like everyone else? Other men bring home money. 

Other men build houses. You bring home only your miserable integrity.

On every bus, on every latrine wall: "Money Sweet Pass All."

Armah does not write about politics with speeches. He writes about it with rot. 

With blocked latrines, decaying wood, filth that won't flush. 

Because that is the moral atmosphere of the post-independence state. The colonialists left, but the extraction did not leave. 

The new black elite learned the old white grammar too well.

Minister Koomson is the apotheosis. Big man. Flash car. House that was not built by salary.

And when Koomson falls after the coup, who helps him escape? The same incorruptible man. 

Through the latrine hole. Through the very filth that Koomson helped create. That is Armah's cruelest joke: even integrity must wade through rot to show mercy.

The Nigerian Cousin

Achebe told us things fall apart when the center cannot hold. 

Emecheta told us the joys of motherhood become burdens when the system extracts more than it returns.

Armah completes the trinity: independence did not birth the beautiful ones. It simply transferred the instruments of accumulation from the white man to Koomson.

In Nigeria we scaled it. 

From cocoa to crude. From gleam to oil block. From bribe to budget padding. 

The logic is identical, only the numbers have more zeros.

So Much And Yet Little

This is where we must be honest, as you have been. There are men today who are doing so much and yet little — exactly Armah's tension.

In Abia, Alex Otti met a state buried in salary arrears, ghost workers, and debt. Forensic audit. No new borrowing. Reports of significant inherited debt reduction. Roads reappearing where people had forgotten roads could exist. That is not Koomson. That is the man refusing the gleam.

In Oyo, Seyi Makinde has done something rarer: built things that are hard to reverse. Amotekun — a sub-national security answer when the center fails. Institutions with teeth. Agribusiness, not just palliative rice. Education and liveability metrics that survive a single tenure. Infrastructure all around.

These are real births. Partial births.

But Armah's point is structural, not personal. 

A good governor can clear arrears. He cannot clear the federal allocation formula. 

He can plug leakages in Umuahia, but cannot plug opacity in Abuja. 

He can build a road in Ibadan and modern bus terminals, but cannot single-handedly fix the incentives that produce ten new Koomsons next door. System won't let him without checkmate.

Peter Obi's 2023 campaign, for many young Nigerians, was the hope that the beautiful ones had finally been born at national scale. The outcome since has illustrated Armah's warning: regime change without system change is just a new driver on the same rotten bus.

Not Yet, Not Never

That is why the title matters. Armah did not write "The Beautiful Ones Will Never Be Born." He wrote 'Are Not Yet Born.'

Last image: a bus, moving, with the misspelled slogan still on it — THE BEAUTYFUL ONES ARE NOT YET BORN — and beside it, a small flower painted. A stubborn, absurd flower.

That is Nigeria today.

Abia's cleanup is a flower. Oyo's institutions are a flower. The young civil servant who still says no to "something for the boys" is a flower.

They prove purity is possible. They also prove how costly it remains.

My earlier essay said: "Okonkwo's rigidity destroys him; Uchendu's adaptability saves the clan."

text:
4. Holy Basil: The Clearing Harmonizer 

Why is this one plant still in almost every Indian home? Considered holy?  

When working through trauma recovery or emotional baggage, the journey often demands more than mental processing…it requires physical, biological, and emotional safety. These heavy states will shift the body into chronic survival states like hypervigilance, emotional overwhelm, or deep nervous system fatigue.

Enter Holy Basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum / Ocimum sanctum), revered in Ayurvedic tradition as Tulsi, “The Incomparable One.” Long cherished as a sacred plant, Tulsi is a master harmonizer for a burdened mind and body. 

Tulsi is classified as a rasayana in Ayurveda: a rejuvenative used to restore vitality after depletion. It is considered sattvic, a quality associated with clarity, presence, and mental purity rather than agitation or dullness. 

It is traditionally said to calm excess vata (the quality associated with anxiety, scattered thinking, and nervous system dysregulation) while also lifting stagnant, heavy states.

Reach for Tulsi when the system has been under prolonged sympathetic load and needs more capacity without being pushed. It tends to settle reactivity while preserving awareness, supporting clarity and presence.

How It Works: 
Trauma alters our stress response system, keeping the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis on high alert. This often manifests as elevated cortisol, anxiety, brain fog, and an inability to settle into rest. 

Human studies on standardized extracts have shown reductions in perceived stress, improvements in sleep quality, and in one trial, lower hair cortisol after several weeks of consistent use. 

Adaptogenic Balance: Tulsi is a primary adaptogen. It helps regulate baseline cortisol levels, taking the edge off acute stress spikes while rebuilding energy reserves over time.
 
Cerebral & Nervous System Tonic: Rich in active compounds like eugenol, rosmarinic acid, and ursolic acid, Holy Basil promotes microcirculation to the brain. This reduces neuroinflammation and eases the cognitive clarity issues (“brain fog”) associated with chronic hyperarousal.
 
Vagal Tone Support: Tulsi helps soothe the sympathetic (“fight-or-flight”) response, gently nudging the nervous system toward ventral vagal safety: the state where connection, emotional integration, and healing take place.

In Hindu tradition, the plant is understood as protective and purifying, both of the physical space and of the mind. Leaves are offered in worship, and dried stems are sometimes made into beads believed to support focus and shield the wearer from negative influences. In this context, Tulsi is not only a medicine but a living presence that supports devotion, clarity, and a sense of being held.

The traditional association with clarity and protection aligns with this use: it is approached as a plant that helps create the conditions for presence rather than one that dissolves or suppresses what is held.

🌿Energetically it is warming, aromatic, and slightly drying, with an affinity the nervous system, heart, brain, and lungs.

This is light, warm, and aromatic nature is indicative when grief, sorrow, or past emotional weight feels heavy and stuck in the chest. Tulsi has the potential to lift “stagnant sadness”. 

Herbalist David Winston has described it as useful for what he calls “stagnant depression”: a state in which a traumatic event has become the organizing center of a person’s life.

Also for those who experience intrusive thoughts or anxiety spirals, tulsi offers a clarifying, grounding effect by anchoring scattered energy back into the body.

This gentle adaptogen with nervine qualities is generally well-tolerated and is often combined with other nervines (such as milky oats, linden, or skullcap) when deeper nervous system restoration is needed.

I will continue to write about the difference between this plant and the previous plant, Milky Oats in this series.

text:
The Mahabharata teaches a powerful moral: A side may possess a larger army, greater warriors and superior weapons, yet lose because power without righteousness, unity and wisdom can become its own weakness.

Why did the Kauravas lose despite their greater strength?

1\. Power without justice — Duryodhana's greatest mistake

Duryodhana refused to give the Pandavas their rightful share of the kingdom, even when peaceful settlement was possible. His ambition became more important than justice.

Lesson: Power can seize a throne, but it cannot automatically earn legitimacy.

2\. Silence in the face of injustice — Draupadi's humiliation

When Draupadi was humiliated in the royal court, many respected elders remained silent or failed to stop the injustice. Their wisdom and status could not excuse their moral failure.

Lesson: Injustice grows not only through the actions of wrongdoers, but also through the silence of those who could challenge them.

3\. A powerful army cannot compensate for bad leadership

The Kauravas had formidable warriors such as Bhishma, Drona and Karna. But their loyalties, rivalries and differing judgments weakened their collective effectiveness. Duryodhana's stubbornness repeatedly undermined opportunities for peace.

Lesson: Numbers create strength; wise leadership, shared purpose and sound judgment turn strength into success.

4\. Great ability without moral independence can become destructive

Bhishma and Drona possessed extraordinary knowledge and ability, yet their allegiance to the Kaurava kingdom placed them on a side whose conduct they had reasons to question.

Lesson: Loyalty to an institution is not always the same as loyalty to justice. Conscience must sometimes challenge authority.

5\. Arrogance prevents a person from learning

Krishna offered peaceful alternatives before the war, but Duryodhana refused meaningful compromise.

Lesson: A leader who mistakes criticism for weakness and compromise for defeat may eventually destroy what they are trying to preserve.

6\. Dharma is more than numbers or outward virtue

The Pandavas were not portrayed as flawless, and the Mahabharata itself contains morally complicated decisions by both sides. Krishna's strategies, including actions that challenge conventional rules of warfare, make the epic more complex than a simple story of good people defeating bad people.

Lesson: The epic invites us to examine justice, consequences, duty and moral responsibility—not merely to count victories and defeats.

 The deeper moral for society

The Kauravas' defeat can be understood as a warning about what happens when ambition overrides justice, when institutions tolerate wrongdoing, and when powerful people refuse to correct their mistakes.

A large army can win battles. Wealth can purchase influence. Fear can silence opposition. But none of these guarantees lasting legitimacy.

The ultimate moral is this:

When power abandons justice, loyalty replaces conscience, and arrogance rejects wisdom, strength itself can become the instrument of defeat.

And one further lesson matters just as much: victory does not automatically prove righteousness, just as defeat does not automatically prove wrongdoing. We must judge actions by their morality and consequences, not merely by who wins.

That is why the Mahabharata remains relevant far beyond the battlefield.

No Singapore citizen has flown to space yet. Vietnam did in 1980, Malaysia in 2007. I'd like Singapore to be next. I'm a Singaporean who has spent 16 years leading APAC tech teams. My goal is Starship Mission 2030 - a roughly 6-day crewed flight around the Moon, targeting 2030, the year Singapore turns 65. 🇸🇬

Why Starship? It's 124 m tall, designed to be fully reusable and refuelled in orbit, and built for trips beyond Earth orbit. That's what could open space to far more people, not just a few.

My plan, in stages:
- Foundations: Starbase visits (2022, 2025) and 5 visits to SpaceX in US
- Training: aerobatics in an Extra 330 (Las Vegas), flight time in Melbourne, PADI Open Water done. Medicals and PPL ground school next

It's early. No seat is booked, and this is a private initiative, not endorsed by @SpaceX. If you're a potential sponsor, or part of Singapore and Asia's space and STEM community, happy to speak. Thanks to those who have already reached out and offered valuable advice.

To the stars, for all.

text:
AI News — Oct 19, 2026

Today's theme: AI's value, people and agents are all getting re-priced, and not by the model benchmarks.

Anthropic is putting equity behind its mission statement. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of its shares go into a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, and the board can add 2% more for every 50% rise in the company's value above a set baseline. It's set up as an LLC, not a charity, so it can fund nonprofits or make direct payouts, and its equity is barred from lobbying or political giving. Anthropic named AI's impact on jobs as one target, on top of the $200M it has already committed there. Counting founder and employee pledges, it says roughly 20% of the company is now earmarked for public benefit.
Why it matters: the bigger Anthropic gets, the bigger the fund's slice. My read: it's a pointed contrast with the usual escalating executive equity awards, and a useful signal to regulators.

Disney is buying https://t.co/ttjWJD3vW2's people, not just its tech. A bankruptcy filing reported by TechCrunch and Bloomberg shows Disney agreed to offer jobs to at least 60 https://t.co/ttjWJD3vW2 employees, most of the workforce including the CEO, at an estimated $60M a year in pay. Its $20M cash bid for the company ($7.5M upfront) is a stalking-horse offer, so other buyers can still top it. https://t.co/ttjWJD3vW2 filed for Chapter 11 on Oct 12.
Why it matters: the acquihire is alive and well, and the talent is priced far above the company itself.

OpenAI says it will build a humanoid robot. Sam Altman told Fortune he expects "a cool demo in 2027," but robots walking the streets are "a few years longer." OpenAI lists 27 robotics roles across actuators, sensors, thermal systems and manufacturing, and its job posts point first at robots that assist skilled workers in infrastructure construction.
Why it matters: OpenAI is stepping into hardware, where Tesla's Optimus and others are already racing. A demo date is not a product date.

The web is starting to close the door on AI agents. The Verge reports Amazon has blocked Meta's Muse shopping agent, Yelp only lets agents in through its paid licensing program, and Delta doesn't let third-party agents book flights. Charles Schwab says it's blocking agents from moving client money and plans read-only access instead.
Why it matters: agents are running into the businesses that own the customer relationship. My read: paid, permissioned access becomes the norm long before open agent browsing does.

Bottom line: this week, capital, talent and access are being priced more carefully than the models themselves.

I just pointed Claude Code to the game URL, asked it to figure it out, then prompted it a bit to improve things.

The tech stack for this to work is:

1. An Oracle VM that runs the script;
2. A Claude API key with some credit. It currently costs about 10 cents a day to keep him running using Haiku (the cheapest model).
3. Find tuning of the bot with Claude Code to make sure it's running optimally. For example, it was using up 2 CPU cores and I was able to lower that to 1% of a CPU core by making it work via API requests instead of the browser. Claude Code did it all, I just prompted it.
4. A Telegram account with an API key so I can chat with the bot.
5. OpenBao to manage secrets. It can be 1Password or Bitwarden or any other password manager so that passwords aren't stored in env files.

If you want to do the same thing, use OpenCode or Claude Code or Codex and roughly prompt it like this:

"Access the URL https://t.co/uaDlkj7GUo. Create a bot that navigates the game and chats with other participants. Help me set up my Telegram for me to communicate with the bot. Have it read the Parano1d documentation so that it can answer questions about it. Create a wallet for the bot and store the keys in my computer. Let me know the address and I'll fund it with 2 NOID."

This should be plenty for it to get started then tweak as you go.

As a tip, Oracle offers free VMs for their Always Free account. The free 1 CPU 1GB RAM is plenty for this. I  recommend it for studying this sort of deployment.

text:
WILLIAM BOYCE THOMPSON: Was an American mining engineer, financier, Republican political figure, and philanthropist. Born in Virginia City, Montana Territory, and raised in Butte.

He made a large fortune developing copper (and other) mines in the West, founded Newmont Mining, and settled in Yonkers, New York.

He built a major estate and established the Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant Research.

Thompson grew up in rough Montana mining towns. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and briefly studied at the Columbia School of Mines before joining his father in mining and lumber ventures.

He later moved east and became a successful mine promoter and stockbroker.

Notable successes included the Shannon Copper Company (linked to Arizona’s large Morenci operations), involvement with Nevada Consolidated (later part of Kennecott), the Magma mine near Superior, Arizona, and the Inspiration Copper Company.

He developed low-grade porphyry copper deposits and high-grade properties, amassing substantial wealth.

In 1916 he founded the Newmont Company (later Newmont Mining/Corporation), a holding company for his interests that grew into a major mining firm.

He also had stakes in other industries (including sulphur, oil, and various promotions) and served as a director of institutions such as Metropolitan Life Insurance Company and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (1914–1919).

He was active in Republican politics (presidential elector, national convention delegate in 1916 and 1920) and declined a potential cabinet post under Harding.

During World War I he supported Belgian relief efforts associated with Herbert Hoover and headed an American Red Cross mission to Russia after the 1917 revolutions.

The famine and instability he witnessed there influenced his later philanthropy focused on plant science and food security.

He received an honorary “Colonel” title from the Red Cross.

In 1912 Thompson built the W. B. Thompson Mansion (also known as Alder Manor), a large Renaissance Revival residence designed by Carrère and Hastings on North Broadway in the Greystone section of Yonkers.

Named after Alder Gulch in Montana, it sat on a substantial property with extensive gardens and offered views of the Hudson River and Palisades.

He and his family (wife Gertrude Hickman Thompson and daughter Margaret) lived there; he died at the estate in 1930 from pneumonia and is buried at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery.

The mansion later served educational and other uses and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Motivated by concerns over food supply and plant science, he founded the Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant Research in 1924 (named for his parents), endowing it generously (reports cite figures in the millions of dollars, with contemporary accounts of substantial investment).

The institute was built across from his mansion in Yonkers with advanced greenhouses and laboratories intended for long-term basic research rather than quick applied results.

It operated in Yonkers for decades before relocating to the Cornell University campus in Ithaca in the late 1970s; it remains an independent research institute focused on plant biology, agriculture, and related fields.

He also established the Boyce Thompson Arboretum near Superior, Arizona (associated with his winter property, Picket Post House), which became a significant botanical garden.

Other gifts included substantial support for Phillips Exeter Academy, libraries and parks in mining communities, and a mineral/gem collection bequeathed to the American Museum of Natural History.

A 1926 New Yorker profile highlighted the Yonkers institute’s sophisticated equipment (including controlled environments and specialized lighting for plant studies) and Thompson’s estate opposite it.

The William Boyce Thompson School (a public PK–8 magnet school at 1061 N. Broadway in Yonkers) is named after him.

His estate was valued in the tens of millions at death (with contemporary estimates of his fortune higher); much went to family, with notable bequests for scientific and cultural purposes.

Newmont Mining continued as a major company, and the plant institute and Arizona arboretum endure as key parts of his legacy.

A 1935 biography, The Magnate by Herman Hagedorn, profiles his life - Thompson rose from Montana mining towns to Wall Street and mining prominence.

Then used much of his fortune for scientific philanthropy centered in Yonkers and Arizona, driven in part by humanitarian concerns about food and agriculture.

text:
Another brainless endeavour by Liberals.  

Starlink is fully operational today with a massive consumer-focused network; Telesat Lightspeed is a planned enterprise/government system not expected to offer commercial service until early 2028.
Current status and scale
•  Starlink: ~11,000+ satellites in low Earth orbit (~550 km altitude), with ongoing rapid deployment (including new higher-capacity V3 satellites). It has roughly 12 million global subscribers and more than 500,000 users in Canada. Coverage reaches most of Canada, including remote and northern areas.
•  Telesat Lightspeed: 0 operational production satellites so far. The planned constellation is 225 satellites (recently expanded from ~156 due to a Canadian military contract). First pathfinder/production launches are targeted for December 2026 on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, with global commercial service expected around Q1 2028. Orbits are higher (~1,000–1,300 km).
Target markets and service model
•  Starlink primarily serves residential/consumer users (plus mobile/RV “Roam,” aviation, maritime, and some enterprise). It is a direct-to-consumer best-effort broadband service. In Canada, residential plans typically run about $75–$150 CAD/month (tiered up to ~400 Mbps priority) with unlimited data and no long-term contracts; hardware is often available as a low-cost or free rental in many areas. Real-world speeds commonly fall in the 100–300+ Mbps range with ~20–40 ms latency.
•  Telesat Lightspeed is designed as a business-to-business (B2B) wholesale and enterprise system for telecom providers, governments, defence, aviation, and maritime users—not direct residential consumers. It emphasises guaranteed service-level agreements (SLAs), Carrier Ethernet (Layer 2) connectivity, optical inter-satellite links for routing control and data sovereignty, and military Ka-band spectrum. It aims to focus capacity where needed in real time and support high-latitude/Arctic operations. No public consumer pricing exists because it is not aimed at households.
Key practical differences
•  Availability and performance today: Starlink is usable now across Canada for homes, cottages, RVs, and remote sites. Telesat cannot replace it for residential users for years; even once live, it is expected to reach most end-users through local telecom partners rather than direct dish sales like Starlink.
•  Sovereignty and Canadian ties: Telesat is Ottawa-based, with substantial Canadian government funding (loans, equity, and a ~$2.3 billion Arctic military communications contract) and satellites built by MDA Space in Montreal. It markets features for secure, sovereign routing. However, a US investment firm owns a significant stake (~35%), and it depends on SpaceX for most launches. Starlink is fully US/SpaceX-controlled.
•  Capacity and economics: Starlink’s far larger constellation and vertical integration (own launches, manufacturing, and rapid iteration) give it a major scale advantage and lower per-bit costs. Telesat’s smaller, higher-orbit design prioritises enterprise-grade reliability, SLAs, and specialised military use over mass consumer volume.
In short, for anyone needing satellite internet in Canada right now (or the next couple of years), Starlink is the practical option. Telesat Lightspeed is positioned as a future sovereign/enterprise alternative, particularly valuable for government and defence needs in the Arctic and elsewhere, but it will not be a direct near-term substitute for Starlink’s consumer service.

text:
@elonmusk 

Canada’s Unsung Role in Building Elon Musk (and Why We Should Have Put a Tariff on Him)

In the summer of 1989, a skinny 17-year-old from Pretoria stepped off a plane in Montreal with little more than a bag of clothes, some books, and a Canadian passport he’d obtained because his mother, Maye, was born in Regina. Canada was the practical doorway to the wider world he wanted, and it turned out to be a better school than he expected.6
He took a bus west and landed with distant cousins on a farm near Waldeck, Saskatchewan. There he tended vegetables, shoveled grain bins, and celebrated his 18th birthday with a homemade cake. Later he moved to Vancouver, learned to run a chainsaw, and then walked into the employment office and asked for the highest-paying job available. That turned out to be cleaning the boiler room of a lumber mill for $18 an hour—roughly triple the usual rate. The work required a hazmat suit, crawling through a narrow tunnel into a chamber full of hot, steaming sludge and residue, and shoveling it back out the same hole. Most people quit within days. Elon lasted the week.7
He later called the conditions a “Dickensian steampunk nightmare.” The story is well documented in Ashlee Vance’s biography and in Musk’s own interviews, including on the Third Row Tesla podcast. What stands out isn’t just the grit; it’s that a kid with almost no money and no local network took the dirtiest, best-paying job on offer and simply showed up until the end.16
Canada gave him more than hard labour. He enrolled at Queen’s University in Kingston, made lasting friendships, and spent two formative years before transferring south to the University of Pennsylvania. By the time he reached the United States, the work ethic and the sense that hard, unglamorous effort was simply part of the deal had already been installed.
Looking back, it’s easy to see the Canadian chapter as a quiet but essential stretch of the journey. The farm, the chainsaw, the boiler, the first real friends, the passport that opened the door—all of it happened here. Perhaps, in hindsight, Canada should have slapped a modest export tariff on him when he finally headed to the States. At least then the rest of us could have claimed a small residual share of the rockets, the cars, and the rest of it. As it stands, the only real claim is the better one: we helped a determined young man get on his feet, and then we watched what he did with the opportunity. That’s not a bad legacy for a cold, practical country.

text:
Peyton Manning’s overall impact on Monday Night Football could be a combination of football education, entertainment, and renewed personality in the broadcast booth. If he replaced Troy Aikman alongside Joe Buck, Manning could bring a different perspective to ESPN’s flagship NFL telecast while drawing on the success of his existing ManningCast. The possibility has received media attention amid uncertainty over Aikman’s contract, but no replacement has been confirmed.

Manning’s biggest contribution would likely be his ability to explain the quarterback’s perspective. He could break down defensive disguises, pre-snap adjustments, protection calls, and passing concepts, helping viewers understand not just what happened but why. His humor and storytelling could also make the broadcast more lively, recalling the combination of football insight and entertainment associated with John Madden’s MNF era.

For Buck, Manning would offer a new partner who could challenge his observations, tell memorable stories, and create a different on-air rhythm. Their chemistry would take time to develop, and Manning would need to adapt his conversational style to the pace of a traditional live broadcast.

Ultimately, Manning could help MNF restore a stronger sense of personality and occasion while making its football analysis more accessible. Rather than simply replacing Aikman, he could give the broadcast a distinct identity built around quarterback intelligence, humor, and behind-the-scenes insight into the game.

text:
A Joe Buck–Peyton Manning pairing could restore several qualities that made Monday Night Football memorable: personality, entertaining football analysis, quarterback insight, and a distinctive broadcast identity. The original MNF booth featuring Frank Gifford, Howard Cosell, and Don Meredith helped establish the program as more than a football game, while the John Madden era demonstrated how detailed analysis and humor could coexist.

Manning could restore the feeling that viewers are learning something new about football every week. His explanations of defensive coverages, audibles, and quarterback decisions could bring greater depth to the broadcast, while his humor and storytelling could make the commentary more entertaining. Unlike the traditional, measured style of Troy Aikman, Manning might offer a more animated perspective without sacrificing technical detail.

Buck would provide the consistency needed to make that approach work. His play-by-play style could balance Manning’s personality, much as Al Michaels balanced Madden’s enthusiasm. Their partnership could also give ESPN a more distinctive identity by combining the polish of a traditional broadcast with the conversational qualities viewers associate with the ManningCast.

Ultimately, Buck and Manning could help restore the sense that Monday night football is an event, not simply another nationally televised game. They would not need to imitate past booths; they could revive their most enduring qualities—chemistry, character, insightful analysis, and entertainment—while creating a new identity for MNF.

#SeniorSundaySpotlight

⭐️ @KenzleiMathews 
💪 Indiana Shockwaves Grayson 18U
🏫 Western Boone Jr-Sr High School
🥎 2B / RHP / C / UTL
👩🏼‍🎓 Class of 2027
🔓 Uncommitted
📚 Intended Major: Nursing or Medical Imaging

When Western Boone needed a catcher, Kenzlei Mathews stepped behind the plate. Catching wasn’t her primary position, but she learned an entirely new role and caught nearly the entire season—not because it was where she wanted to play, but because it was where her team needed her.

That season ended on the field at Purdue University, where Western Boone competed in the 2026 IHSAA Class 2A State Championship and finished as state runner-up. Kenzlei will never forget looking around and realizing how far her team had come. They may not have brought home the title, but they made school history—and proved what can happen when a group continues fighting for one another.

Softball has taught Kenzlei that she is stronger than she sometimes gives herself credit for. She doesn’t have to be the biggest or most naturally talented player on the field to make a difference. She must be willing to work, learn and refuse to give up. A switch hitter, slapper and true utility player, she has played all nine positions and takes pride in being someone her team can count on wherever she is needed.

Her parents have supported her since she began playing at three years old, while a long list of coaches has helped shape different parts of her game and mindset. They taught her new positions, developed her as a switch hitter, trusted her in meaningful roles and reminded her that “I can” is the only mindset to carry. Their influence has helped Kenzlei become a more confident player—but also a more accountable teammate.

The hardest part of her journey was learning that growth sometimes requires decisions that break your own heart. After navigating health challenges, setbacks and self-doubt, Kenzlei made the difficult decision to leave Shockwaves Raney—a team she considered family—to step outside her comfort zone and continue pursuing college softball. A different jersey will never erase the friendships, memories or love she has for those teammates. The experience taught her that she can chase new dreams without forgetting the people who helped her build them.

Her advice to younger athletes is to never allow someone else to decide how far they can go. Bad games, mistakes and rejection will happen, but they do not have to define the journey. Work when no one is watching, remain coachable, keep learning and never compare your path to someone else’s.

Kenzlei hopes her coaches and teammates remember her as the girl who would do absolutely anything for her team—the player who cared more about helping her teammates succeed than which position appeared beside her name. Softball has given her a second family, lifelong friendships and the strength to believe in herself when life gets hard. Now she is searching for a college that offers Nursing or Medical Imaging and a positive, competitive softball family where she can contribute, grow and continue chasing her dream. ❤️🥎
